opus-5.5.text:
I think the Industrial Revolution is probably the best reference point we have, though it's imperfect. Before roughly 1700 or 1800, the world economy grew at something like a tenth of a percent a year. Afterwards, growth settled at around two to three percent annually in the frontier economies. That's a roughly tenfold to thirtyfold acceleration in the growth rate, and it happened over a historically short window. So the first lesson is that these regime changes really do happen. The growth rate we're used to isn't a law of nature; it's a feature of a particular era.

The second lesson concerns the mechanism. Many economists, myself included, find the semi-endogenous growth story compelling: ideas drive growth, ideas are produced by people, and more output means more people, which means more ideas. That feedback loop explains a lot of the long-run acceleration in human history. The demographic transition partly broke it, because once people got richer they stopped converting extra output into extra population. Output kept growing, but the number of researchers didn't scale with it the way it used to.

What makes AI interesting is that it potentially restores that loop, and in a much tighter form. If AI systems can substitute for human labor broadly, including in research and development, then you can turn compute into workers. Compute is something you can accumulate by investing output. You get back the feedback where more output means more "minds," which means more ideas and more output. That's essentially the dynamic that drove accelerating growth historically, except now it's not bottlenecked by human population growth or by the twenty-odd years it takes to raise and train a person.

So when people ask whether thirty percent annual growth is crazy, I'd point to the Industrial Revolution and say: by pre-modern standards, two or three percent would have seemed just as crazy. A medieval economist projecting forward would never have predicted it.

That said, I'd be careful about the analogy in a few ways. The Industrial Revolution was quite gradual in calendar time; it took many decades to diffuse, and early on measured growth was surprisingly modest. You had to build factories and railways, reorganize labor, and develop institutions. I expect AI to face analogous bottlenecks: physical capital, energy, regulatory approval, the parts of the economy that are hard to automate. Those will shape how quickly the transition actually shows up in GDP. One thing people often miss is that the sectors you can't automate tend to become the binding constraint, and their share of the economy grows. The Industrial Revolution teaches us about the potential for a step change, but also about how messy and uneven the actual unfolding tends to be.

r001.rationale: It says the Industrial Revolution required building factories and railways, reorganizing labor, and developing institutions, presenting changes in infrastructure, labor, and institutions as jointly needed for the transformation.

r002.rationale: It identifies AI systems as a driver while also naming compute investment, physical capital, energy, regulatory approval, and hard-to-automate sectors as factors shaping the economic transition.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the Industrial Revolution is maybe the single most useful reference point we have, because it's the one time in history where the growth regime actually changed. Before roughly 1800, the global economy was growing at something like a tenth of a percent per year, maybe a bit more in the leading economies. And then over the course of about a century, you see this transition to the two or three percent per year that we now think of as normal. So output doubling every twenty-five or thirty years instead of every several centuries. That's a change in the rate of change, not just a one-off boost in the level, and I think that's the right frame for thinking about AI.

What drove that shift? There are a bunch of stories, but the one I find most compelling is about the economics of ideas. Before the Industrial Revolution you have this Malthusian dynamic where more people means more innovation, but also more mouths to feed, so the gains from better technology get eaten up by population growth and living standards stay flat. At some point you get enough of a positive feedback between population, ideas, and output that the economy escapes that trap. More people produce more ideas, those ideas raise output, and that supports more people and more research, and the whole thing accelerates. Then eventually fertility declines, population growth decouples from income, and we settle into the steady exponential we've had for the past hundred and fifty years.

The reason this matters for AI is that the key bottleneck in that story is the number of minds doing research and development. Human population growth is now slow and in many places negative, and the semi-endogenous growth models say that's why we don't see further acceleration. If AI systems can substitute for human researchers and workers, and if you can scale the number of those systems by just building more compute, then you've essentially reconnected output to the growth of the "population" of idea producers. You reinvest output into more compute, more compute does more R&D and more production, and you get the same kind of feedback loop that produced the Industrial Revolution, except the input is capital rather than people, and capital can be accumulated far faster than humans can be born and educated.

So the analogy gives you two things. First, it tells you that growth regime changes are real, they've happened before, and they don't require magic. Second, it gives you a mechanism, and when you plug AI into the standard models, the mechanism points toward growth rates that could be an order of magnitude higher than what we have now, say twenty or thirty percent per year rather than two or three.

I'd also stress where the analogy is imperfect. The Industrial Revolution took a century or more to unfold, and a lot of that was because it depended on human learning, institutions, and demographic shifts that move slowly. With AI the relevant inputs are things like chips and energy and data centers, which can be scaled over years rather than generations. So if anything, the lesson is that the transition could be considerably faster, and that the main things slowing it down would be physical bottlenecks and regulation rather than the inherent pace of human adaptation.

r001.rationale: The response explains the Industrial Revolution through population, ideas, and output feedback, but does not attribute it to complementary changes across multiple economic sectors.

r002.rationale: It describes AI systems and compute as part of the growth mechanism, and mentions infrastructure and regulation as constraints, but does not clearly state that increasingly capable AI systems are one of multiple factors driving the transformation.

astra-6.text:
I think the Industrial Revolution is useful because it shows that the growth rate of the economy isn’t some fixed feature of the world. You can change the process by which production happens and get a sustained increase in growth, rather than just a one-time increase in income.

But there’s also an important difference. During the Industrial Revolution, we became much better at using machines and energy to perform physical tasks. We still relied on humans to invent those machines, organize production, and figure out what to do next. So even as you accumulated more capital, you had this constraint imposed by the availability of human labor and ingenuity.

AI could relax that constraint. If you can reproduce the work of a scientist or an engineer by building more computing infrastructure, then investment can expand the supply of the very capabilities that make further investment productive. Better AI could help develop better chips, better algorithms, and better ways of producing things. That creates the possibility of a much stronger feedback loop.

The lesson isn’t that this necessarily happens overnight. The Industrial Revolution also illustrates how much complementary investment and organizational change can matter. You need to integrate a technology into actual production. And if AI makes some tasks extraordinarily cheap while other essential tasks remain difficult to automate, those remaining tasks can become bottlenecks.

So I’d use the Industrial Revolution as evidence that a technological transformation can change the long-run growth regime, but I wouldn’t assume that its pace or magnitude gives us a reliable template for AI. Automating the process of technological improvement itself would be a further, quite consequential step.

r001.rationale: The response says complementary investment and organizational change matter, but it does not attribute the Industrial Revolution’s transformation to changes across multiple sectors.

r002.rationale: It presents increasingly capable AI as part of a broader transformation, alongside complementary investment, organizational change, production integration, and tasks that may remain bottlenecks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the Industrial Revolution is useful because it shows that the rate of economic growth isn’t fixed. For most of human history, improvements in technology didn’t translate into sustained increases in income per person. Then we moved into a regime where each generation could expect to be substantially richer than the last. AI raises the possibility of another change in that growth regime.

But there’s an important difference. Industrial machinery substituted for particular kinds of physical work, while humans remained essential for figuring out what to build, organizing production, and inventing better technologies. If AI can substitute for those cognitive tasks, it could automate parts of the process that generates economic growth itself.

Think about research. Today, producing more ideas requires training and employing more researchers, which is expensive and slow. If you could instead expand research effort by making more copies of an AI system, then investment in computing could lead to better technology, including better computing and better AI. That creates the possibility of a much stronger feedback loop.

The Industrial Revolution also cautions against expecting everything to happen immediately. A powerful technology still needs complementary investments, new organizations, and changes in how people work. With AI, the key question is which of those constraints remain binding as cognitive labor becomes cheaper. You could have very rapid progress in software and research while construction, energy, and physical production take longer to catch up.

r001.rationale: The response says the Industrial Revolution involved machinery replacing some physical work while people remained essential for other tasks, and notes that technologies need complementary investments and organizational changes. It does not clearly attribute the Industrial Revolution’s economic transformation to complementary changes across multiple sectors.

r002.rationale: The response presents AI as a potential driver of faster growth while also identifying complementary investments, organizational changes, and changes in how people work as necessary factors.
